newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. envoy calls Serb retaliation "dangerous".
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy calls Serb retaliation "dangerous".

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations said on Monday that Bosnian Serb retaliation for a tougher international approach to indicted war criminals was intolerable and dangerous.

International monitors and peacekeeping soldiers have been targeted by a series of small-scale explosions over the past 10 days since a NATO raid on two Serb suspects wanted by the United Nations for war crimes.
"Recent provocations in Republika Srpska (the Bosnian Serb republic) are intolerable and if not ended could pull us down an extremely dangerous road," ambassador Bill Richardson told reporters.
He said the commander of the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR), U.S. General William Crouch, had assured him that SFOR would "not be deterred from carrying out its mission".
No explosions were reported on Sunday night for the first time in a week. On Saturday night a European Union monitor's car was damaged in a bombing.

Richardson said Serb authorities risked losing out on reconstruction aid at a fund-raising conference this week if they failed to uphold their obligations to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague as set out in the Dayton peace agreement.

"Failure to fulfil the demands and requirements of Dayton including handing over indicted war criminals to The Hague tribunal will adversely effect the decisions on aid made at the donors' conference and subsequently," he said.
Richardson accused the Bosnian Serb media, under the control of hardliners loyal to former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, of whipping up hostility towards SFOR.
"This kind of a propaganda campaign only serves the interest of a tiny clique who are bent on maintaining their grip on power," he said.

The U.S. envoy also announced that Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and the Moslem chairman of the Bosnian presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, had agreed to hold talks on August 6 after several months of delays.
The meeting concerns the formation of an integrated police force in the Mostar region which has been the subject of a long-running dispute between rival Croat and Moslem communities.
